content: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning? {{v:2}} My God, I cry in the daytime, but you don’t answer; in the night season, and am not silent. {{v:3}} But you are holy, you who inhabit the praises of Israel. {{v:4}} Our fathers trusted in you. They trusted, and you delivered them. {{v:5}} They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed. {{v:6}} But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. {{v:7}} All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, {{v:8}} “He trusts in the LORD. Let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.” {{v:9}} But you brought me out of the womb. You made me trust while at my mother’s breasts. {{v:10}} I was thrown on you from my mother’s womb. You are my God since my mother bore me. {{v:11}} Don’t be far from me, for trouble is near. For there is no one to help. {{v:12}} Many bulls have surrounded me. Strong bulls of Bashan have encircled me. {{v:13}} They open their mouths wide against me, lions tearing prey and roaring. {{v:14}} I am poured out like water. All my bones are out of joint. My heart is like wax. It is melted within me. {{v:15}} My strength is dried up like a potsherd. My tongue sticks to the roof of my mouth. You have brought me into the dust of death. {{v:16}} For dogs have surrounded me. A company of evildoers have enclosed me. They have pierced my hands and feet. {{v:17}} I can count all of my bones. They look and stare at me. {{v:18}} They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing. {{v:19}} But don’t be far off, LORD. You are my help. Hurry to help me! {{v:20}} Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog. {{v:21}} Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, you have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen. {{v:22}} I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you. {{v:23}} You who fear the LORD, praise him! All you descendants of Jacob, glorify him! Stand in awe of him, all you descendants of Israel! {{v:24}} For he has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard. {{v:25}} My praise of you comes in the great assembly. I will pay my vows before those who fear him. {{v:26}} The humble shall eat and be satisfied. They shall praise the LORD who seek after him. Let your hearts live forever. {{v:27}} All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you. {{v:28}} For the kingdom is the LORD’s. He is the ruler over the nations. {{v:29}} All the rich ones of the earth shall eat and worship. All those who go down to the dust shall bow before him, even he who can’t keep his soul alive. {{v:30}} Posterity shall serve him. Future generations shall be told about the Lord. {{v:31}} They shall come and shall declare his righteousness to a people that shall be born, for he has done it.

facets.text: The psalm opens with the anguished cry "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"—a prayer that voices the terrible experience of God's felt absence in the midst of suffering. Yet this is not a cry of unbelief but of faith stretched to its limit, for the sufferer still addresses God as "my God" and continues to pray without ceasing. The complaint is directed to God, not away from him, revealing that lament itself can be an act of trust.
facets.question: How can crying out that God has forsaken me still be an act of faith?

facets.text: Jesus prays the opening words of this psalm from the cross, making Psalm 22 the definitive Passion psalm of the New Testament. By taking these words upon his lips, Christ shows that his cry of abandonment is the prayer of the righteous sufferer who remains united to the Father even in the depths of desolation, and that the whole psalm—including its triumphant conclusion—is fulfilled in him. The Church reads the entire arc from suffering to vindication as a prophecy of the Passion and Resurrection.
facets.question: Why did Jesus pray Psalm 22 on the cross?

facets.text: The detailed description of the sufferer—pierced hands and feet, bones out of joint, thirst that dries the tongue, garments divided by casting lots, mockers shaking their heads—reads as a startlingly precise foreshadowing of the crucifixion centuries before that mode of execution existed in Israel. The Gospels deliberately echo these details to show that Christ's Passion unfolds according to the Scriptures. This is prophecy as providential correspondence, where the ancient prayer and the historical event illuminate one another.
facets.question: What details in Psalm 22 foretell the crucifixion of Christ?

facets.text: The sufferer roots his hope in God's covenant faithfulness, recalling that "our fathers trusted in you" and were delivered, and that God has held him "since my mother bore me." His plea rests not on his own merit but on God's proven character and lifelong care from the womb onward. Prayer in distress draws its confidence from remembering God's steadfast history of salvation.
facets.question: On what basis does the psalmist hope for deliverance while suffering?

facets.text: The psalm turns decisively from lament to praise: "I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you." The one who felt abandoned proclaims that God "has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted" but heard his cry. This movement teaches that God's answer transforms suffering into public thanksgiving, and the Church sees here the fruit of the Resurrection announced within the assembly of the redeemed.
facets.question: How does Psalm 22 move from abandonment to thanksgiving?

facets.text: The psalm's vision widens to universal and eschatological scope: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD... For the kingdom is the LORD's." The vindication of the one sufferer becomes the occasion for all nations to worship, embracing even the poor who "eat and be satisfied" and those who "go down to the dust." The tradition sees here the catholic reach of redemption and a Eucharistic satisfying of the humble in the kingdom Christ inaugurates.
facets.question: How does the suffering of one person in Psalm 22 lead to the salvation of all nations?

facets.text: The psalm's final phrase, "he has done it," declares the saving work as accomplished, a completed act that future generations will proclaim to a people yet unborn. Christian tradition hears an anticipation of Christ's own "It is finished," understanding the sufferer's vindication as a deed God has definitively wrought. Salvation is presented not as human achievement but as God's finished work, handed on across generations.
facets.question: What is the meaning of the declaration "he has done it" at the end of Psalm 22?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Psalm 22 is the great psalm of the righteous sufferer, moving from a cry of abandonment through vivid affliction to vindication, universal worship, and God's finished saving work—read by the Church as prophecy of Christ's Passion and Resurrection.

[DEVOTIONAL | traditional]: The opening cry of forsakenness is a prayer of faith stretched to its limit, addressing God even in his felt absence, showing lament itself as trust.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Jesus prays these words from the cross, making the whole psalm—from desolation to triumph—a prophecy of his Passion and Resurrection.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: Pierced hands and feet, dislocated bones, thirst, mockery, and garments divided by lot foreshadow the crucifixion, which the Gospels present as fulfilling Scripture.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The sufferer's hope rests on God's covenant faithfulness to the fathers and his lifelong care from the womb, not on personal merit.
[DEVOTIONAL | explicit]: The psalm turns from lament to public praise, declaring that God heard the afflicted, a movement the Church links to the Resurrection announced in the assembly.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The one sufferer's vindication expands to universal, eschatological worship of all nations and the satisfying of the humble, seen as the catholic and Eucharistic reach of redemption.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: The closing \"he has done it\" declares salvation as God's finished work, anticipating Christ's \"It is finished,\" handed on to unborn generations.
